49_Ph2q6uIM.name: What Did Ancient Humans Actually Do All Day?
segs: This morning, a machine screamed at you
until you woke up. You silenced it, and
from that second, your day was already
decided. Where you had to be, what you
had to finish, how many hours belong to
someone else. And tonight, before you
sleep, you'll set that same machine to
scream at you again. Now, rewind 50,000
years. A man wakes up in the morning
light with no alarm, no schedule, and
nowhere he has to be. He owns a spear,
two animal hides, and a fire. And he
sits up, stretches, and asks himself a
question you have never once been free
enough to ask. What should I do today?
Now, your brain is already fighting
this. It's telling you no, ancient life
was brutal, short, and desperate. Every
second was survival. That's what
everyone believed. For centuries, that
was the official story. But the proof
that it's wrong was lying buried in the
ground the entire time. And when
scientists finally dug it up, it flipped
everything upside down. And that opens
up a mystery. Because you live
surrounded by machines built to save
time. Washing machines, dishwashers,
microwaves, cars, every one of them was
invented to give you more free hours.
So, how does a man with none of that, no
technology at all, end up with more free
time than you? What did he actually do
all day that you can't? And where did
all of your time go? To answer that, we
have to start in the ground. Because
somewhere in the Middle East,
archaeologists are digging. And over the
years, from the same region, they pull
up two human skeletons. They lived a few
thousand years apart. That's close
enough to compare them, but far enough
that they come from two completely
different worlds. The first skeleton is
tall. The bones are thick and strong.
The teeth are worn, but healthy. Almost
no cavities. The joints are clean. This
was a body that ate well, moved in
varied ways, and never got ground down
by one repeated motion. The second
skeleton tells a harder story. The teeth
are full of cavities. The spine shows
arthritis. The specific damage you get
from bending and grinding through the
same motion thousands of times, year
after year. And this person died
younger. So, which one is which? Take a
guess. Most people point to the tall,
healthy skeleton and say that's the
modern one. The farmer with tools and
stored food and a roof over his head.
And the short, broken one, that must be
the caveman. The guy scraping by in the
wild with a spear. But it's the
opposite. The strong skeleton belonged
to the hunter-gatherer. The wrecked one
belonged to the farmer, the person from
the era we call progress. And this isn't
one weird pair of bones. Archaeologists
have run this comparison at sites all
over the world, and wherever farming
replaced hunting and gathering, the same
pattern shows up in the ground.
Generations got shorter than the ones
before them. Their teeth rotted, their
spines wore down, and their lives ended
earlier. Think about what that means.
Your skeleton is a diary. It records how
hard you worked, how well you ate, how
your body was used, and it holds that
record for thousands of years. And the
diaries say the people with nothing but
spears were living lives than the people
who came after them with farms, storage,
and villages. But bones can only tell
you so much. They can prove the work was
lighter. They can't show you how a
normal day actually went. So, let me
walk you through one. You wake up at
dawn on your own because your body got
the sleep it needed. The fire from last
night is still burning in the middle of
camp, and people are already sitting
around it eating leftover meat and nuts,
talking about where the water is good
and where the animal tracks were
spotted. That's the whole morning plan,
and when it's decided, it's decided by
everyone. And today, nobody needs to
hunt. The last hunt was 2 days ago, and
there's still plenty of food. So, a few
people go out to gather plants, and you
spend the morning on your tools. You
sharpen your spear, and you work a stiff
hide until it turns soft. You do this
because skill earns respect here, not
because someone told you to. And by
early afternoon, everything that needed
doing is already done. 2 days later, the
meat runs low, so today you hunt. And
real hunting looks nothing like the
movies. You never chase the animal
because it's faster than you, and it
always will be. Instead, you follow it
at a steady walking pace for hours. Your
body can sweat and cool itself while it
moves. The animal can't, so it keeps
sprinting, keeps overheating, and keeps
getting weaker until it finally
collapses, and you walk up to it. You
were never the fastest thing out there.
You were the only thing that never has
to stop. The hunt takes the whole day,
and it's the hardest work this life asks
of you. But one good hunt feeds the camp
for days. So, tomorrow the free time
starts again. And at this point, you're
probably thinking this sounds too good
to be real. It sounds like a fantasy
someone invented about the past. So,
let's deal with that because one man had
the exact same doubt and he did
something about it. In 1963, an
anthropologist named Richard Lee walked
into the Kalahari Desert on the edge of
Botswana. It's one of the harshest
places on Earth a human being can live.
He went there to study the Ju/'hoansi,
one of the last groups still living the
old way, hunting animals and gathering
plants with no farms and no stores. Lee
expected to find misery. That was the
official story in every textbook that
life before farming meant working every
daylight hour just to barely survive.
But instead of assuming it, he decided
to count it. He followed people around
with a notebook and a stopwatch and he
recorded how they spent every single
hour, day after day, for weeks. Lee came
back with a number that nobody believed.
These people were spending about 17
hours a week getting food and that's not
17 hours a day. That's 17 hours across
the entire week, which comes out to
about two and a half days of work. Every
hour after that belonged to them. For
comparison, you'll cross 17 hours of
work by Wednesday afternoon. Now, maybe
the Ju/'hoansi were just one lucky group
in one lucky spot. That's a fair doubt
and scientists had it, too. So, they
went and ran the same count on other
groups still living the old way. They
checked the Hadza in Tanzania, then the
Ache in Paraguay, then the Martu in
Australia. Three groups on three
different continents and every single
time, the answer came back between 15
and 20 hours a week. That was the full
cost of staying alive. But here's the
part nobody tells you. The most
important hours in that whole week were
not the hunting hours. They were the
lazy-looking hours that came after
because those hours were doing a bigger
job than food. It's afternoon and the
camp has slowed down. People sit in the
shade and talk. They play with the kids
and they groom each other, picking
through hair while the conversation
drifts. Next to you, someone is drilling
tiny holes through seashells to string
into a necklace. Someone else is carving
a design into a piece of bone and that
design has no purpose at all except to
look good. And this isn't a guess about
how they filled their time. At Blombos
Cave in South Africa, archaeologists
found shell beads that are over 70,000
years old, small sea snail shells with
holes carefully drilled through them
made to be worn. The coast was a long
walk from where these people lived. So,
someone made that trip, collected the
shells, carried them home, and then sat
for hours drilling holes with stone
tools, just to make something beautiful.
And in 2008, in a cave in Germany,
researchers dug up a flute carved from a
vulture's wing bone. It's 40,000 years
old, and it has five finger holes spaced
for actual musical notes. So, someone in
the Ice Age understood music well enough
to build an instrument, and someone had
enough free time to learn to play it.
But the beads and the flute point at
something bigger, because this world has
no money, no police, and no courts. So,
ask yourself, what actually keeps you
alive here when your hunt fails, or when
you get sick, or when you break your leg
and can't walk for a month? The answer
is other people. That's the entire
safety net. If people like you, they
feed you when you have nothing. But if
they don't like you, then nobody owes
you anything, and you starve. So, all
those lazy afternoon hours of talking
and joking and grooming were actually an
investment in the only insurance this
world has. The anthropologist James
Suzman found that Ju/'hoansi adults
spend around 6 hours every single day on
pure social time. Because in this world,
your relationships are your bank
account, your hospital, and your
pension, all at once. Then the sun goes
down. And here's where it gets really
interesting, because the best hours of
the day haven't even started yet. In
2014, an anthropologist named Polly
Wiessner published a study that might
explain where human culture itself comes
from. She had recordings of Ju/'hoansi
conversations collected across decades,
and she sorted all of them by one simple
thing. Was it said during the day or at
night? The daytime talk turned out to be
practical. People discussed where the
animal tracks were, which plants were
ready to gather, and who wasn't sharing
fairly. It was basically logistics and
gossip. But at night, around the fire,
the talking changed completely. 81% of
the firelight conversation turned into
stories. People told myths about how the
world began, tales of ancestors who did
impossible things, and jokes that ran
long into the dark. And notice what kind
of stories these are. Gods and spirits,
the past and the future, none of that
comes out of a scared, hungry mind.
Those stories only show up when your
stomach is full and your body is safe.
So, the fire was doing more than cooking
food and keeping predators away. It
created the first hours in human history
where the mind was completely free. And
Weisner argued that this is exactly
where culture was born, not in the
middle of the work, but in the quiet
hours after it. And when the fire burned
low, even sleep worked differently.
Before artificial light existed, humans
didn't sleep in one long block.
Historical records and modern sleep
experiments both show the same pattern.
People slept about 4 hours, then woke up
for an hour or two in the middle of the
night. And they stayed calm in that
darkness, thinking or talking quietly
until sleep came back for another 4
hours. That quiet hour in the middle was
completely normal for thousands of
generations. Today, you wake up at 2:00
a.m. and call it insomnia. Your body
might just be doing the oldest thing it
knows. So, now you've seen the whole
picture. Food took a few hours, people
took the afternoon, stories took the
night, and sleep came in two calm
halves. That was the human schedule for
hundreds of thousands of years. Then,
about 10,000 years ago, somebody planted
a seed. And that's the moment your time
started disappearing. It happened in the
Middle East, in a region called the
Fertile Crescent, when humans started
planting grain and keeping animals
instead of hunting and gathering. And on
paper, farming sounds like a massive
upgrade. You get more food, you get
control, and you never have to follow an
antelope for 6 hours again. But farming
is a trap, and here's exactly how it
snapped shut. Farming produces more
food. More food means more babies
survive, so the population grows. A
bigger population needs more food, so
you plant more fields. More fields means
more work. And then the lock clicks.
Once your group is too big to feed by
hunting and gathering, the old life
can't carry you anymore. You can never
go back. You're in, permanently. And so
is every generation born after you. And
the workload explodes. Now, there's
plowing, planting, weeding, harvesting,
storing, and guarding it all, season
after season, forever. And remember the
second skeleton from the beginning, the
one with the rotten teeth and the
worn-out spine that died young? That
skeleton is what this new life did to
people. The first farmers worked harder
and lived worse than the
hunter-gatherers before them, and they
couldn't leave. And the trap kept
tightening. Big farming villages
produced specialists, potters, tool
makers, weavers. Specialists needed
trade, and trade built cities. Then
cities brought soldiers, priests, and
tax collectors. And eventually they
brought a brand new idea in human
history. For the first time ever, your
hours could belong to someone else, sold
off in exchange for food you no longer
knew how to find on your own. So nobody
stole your time in one dramatic night.
It was traded away slowly, one
generation at a time, in a deal that no
one alive today ever got the chance to
refuse. The alarm that screamed at you
this morning is just the latest payment.
For hundreds of thousands of years,
humans worked 15 to 20 hours a week, and
the skeletons in the ground prove it.
The afternoons went into craft and
beauty, and the relationships that kept
everyone alive. The nights went into
firelight stories, where culture itself
was born, and sleep came in two calm
halves. Then farming arrived, the
population trap locked behind us, and
step by step our hours stopped being
ours. Today, you'll spend about 90,000
hours of your life working. You make art
only if there's anything left of you
after your job. They made art in the
middle of an ordinary afternoon. You
network for career advantage. They spent
6 hours a day with people they loved,
and it counted as survival. You chase
success, savings, retirement, some
finish line where you finally get your
time back. They were already standing on
that finish line. They were born on it.
Every morning, they woke up with no
alarm and no schedule. And they asked
themselves the one question you have
never been free enough to ask. You are
working your entire existence to someday
retire into that life. They lived it
from their first day to their last. And
they would find it very strange that you
traded it all away for a screaming alarm
and a promise.
